title: Lesson 9: Genetics NEA Task 1: Huntington's disease inheritance (Ben case study)
courseName: OCR Level 3 Cambridge Advanced National (AAQ) in Human Biology - Unit F172: Genetics
focus: Huntington's Disease Inheritance, CAG Triplet Repeats, Striatal Neuronal Degeneration, Genetic Anticipation, and Academic Research & Referencing for NEA Task 1
deliverable: Complete the synoptic NEA Task 1 portfolio scaffold: analyze Ben's clinical case study (autosomal dominant transmission, 50% inheritance risk across all 3 children, CAG expansion mechanisms, and striatal MSN apoptosis), evaluate genetic testing and reproductive ethics (presymptomatic testing in minors, prenatal CVS/amniocentesis, and PGD/IVF), and construct an academic literature review with full Harvard referencing.

objectives.knowledge: Explain how CAG repeat expansions in the HTT gene cause mutant huntingtin protein aggregation, selective striatal MSN apoptosis, and motor chorea, defining genetic anticipation.
objectives.application: Apply autosomal dominant inheritance principles (Punnett square cross Hh x hh) to calculate transmission probabilities (50% per child) and evaluate clinical testing pathways for Ben's family.
objectives.evaluation: Evaluate ethical dilemmas in predictive testing of minors versus prenatal diagnosis (CVS/amniocentesis) and PGD/IVF, applying CRAAP criteria and Harvard referencing to NEA Task 1 evidence.

terminology.def: An unstable tandem repeat of Cytosine-Adenine-Guanine in exon 1 of the HTT gene encoding an expanded polyglutamine (polyQ) tract.
Pathological property where mutant huntingtin protein misfolds, aggregates, and destroys striatal GABAergic medium spiny neurons.
A pattern of monogenic inheritance where a single copy of a mutant allele on a non-sex chromosome is sufficient to cause the disease.
The phenomenon where symptoms manifest at an earlier age and with greater clinical severity in successive generations due to meiotic repeat expansion.
Pronounced repeat expansion occurring during spermatogenesis due to continuous germline replication slippage, risking juvenile HD.
Testing in vitro embryos prior to uterine implantation, selecting only unaffected (hh) embryos to prevent disease transmission.

theoryPoints: Case Study Grounding (Ben): Adopted background explains the absence of family history; 40-year-old presentation reflects classic midlife choreiform onset with bilateral striatal atrophy on brain MRI.

Molecular & Cellular Mechanism: Unstable CAG expansion (>=40 repeats) in HTT encodes polyglutamine tract; mutant protein misfolding sequesters transcription factors (CBP), decreases BDNF, and triggers striatal MSN apoptosis.

Transmission & Anticipation Risk: Autosomal dominant cross (Hh x hh) gives a 50% recurrence risk for each child (6yo daughter, 3yo son, unborn baby); paternal transmission risks meiotic slippage expansion and earlier juvenile onset.
Coursework Skills for NEA Task 1: Rigorous academic literature search (PubMed/NICE), source critique using CRAAP criteria, and accurate Harvard author-date citation formatting.

workedExample.title: Ben's Family Genetic Risk & Clinical Pathway Scaffolding
workedExample.subtitle: Constructing the Mendelian cross, evaluating anticipation, and planning clinical testing

steps.label: Step 1: Parental Genotype Assignment
steps.detail: Ben is diagnosed with HD and is heterozygous (Hh). His wife is clinically unaffected with no family history, giving genotype hh.

steps.label: Step 2: Punnett Square Cross (Hh x hh)
steps.detail: Gametes: Ben produces 50% H and 50% h; Wife produces 100% h. Offspring genotypes: 50% Hh (affected), 50% hh (unaffected). Each child has an independent 50% (1 in 2) risk.

steps.label: Step 3: Paternal Anticipation Evaluation
steps.detail: Because Ben is the biological father, meiotic DNA polymerase slippage during spermatogenesis can expand his CAG tract (e.g. from 42 to >55 repeats), exposing his children to earlier-onset or juvenile Huntington's disease.

steps.label: Step 4: Clinical & Reproductive Testing Plan
steps.detail: Presymptomatic testing for the 6yo and 3yo is deferred until age 18 (autonomy/right not to know); prenatal testing (CVS at 11-14 wks or amniocentesis at 15-20 wks) is evaluated for the unborn fetus; PGD with IVF is proposed for future reproductive planning.

hingeQuestions.question: Ben asks his genetic counsellor whether having two healthy children already means their third, unborn child has a lower chance of inheriting Huntington's disease. What is the scientifically accurate response?
options: Yes, because the binomial probability of having three affected children is only 12.5%
No, because each conception is an independent event with an unvarying 50% probability of inheriting the mutant HTT allele
Yes, because maternal alleles compensate for paternal mutations in later pregnancies
No, the risk actually increases to 75% for the third child
hingeQuestions.explanation: In autosomal dominant monogenic inheritance, each conception represents an independent meiotic segregation event. The outcome of previous pregnancies has zero effect on subsequent pregnancies (each child faces an exact 50% risk).

hingeQuestions.question: Why do UK clinical genetics guidelines recommend AGAINST predictive genetic testing for Ben's 6-year-old daughter and 3-year-old son?
options: Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) cannot amplify DNA from children under 10 years old
Huntington's disease testing requires full adult skeletal maturity for accurate results
To protect the child's future autonomy and 'right not to know' their genetic destiny, given that no preventative childhood intervention exists for this adult-onset condition
Because adoption laws prohibit testing biological offspring
hingeQuestions.explanation: International and UK clinical consensus dictates that presymptomatic testing for adult-onset conditions without childhood preventative treatments should be deferred until the individual reaches the age of majority (18 years) to make an informed, autonomous decision.

hingeQuestions.question: Which molecular mechanism explains why genetic anticipation in Huntington's disease is significantly more pronounced when inherited from an affected father compared to an affected mother?
options: The HTT gene is located on the Y chromosome
Spermatogenesis involves continuous lifelong germline cell divisions, leading to frequent replication slippage and repeat expansion in secondary hairpin structures
Oocytes actively methylate and excise CAG repeat codons during meiosis I
Mitochondrial DNA accelerates polyglutamine translation in males
hingeQuestions.explanation: Sperm production involves hundreds of cell divisions throughout male adult life, creating vast opportunities for DNA polymerase replication slippage across tandem repetitive sequences, whereas female gametogenesis involves far fewer divisions.

examQuestion.question: Ben, a 40-year-old adopted teacher, has been diagnosed with early-stage Huntington's disease following symptoms of chorea. He and his wife have two young children (aged 6 and 3) and are expecting a third child. (a) Explain the molecular and cellular mechanism by which a CAG triplet repeat expansion in the HTT gene causes neuronal damage, and explain why his children are at risk of genetic anticipation. (b) Explain how Huntington's disease is inherited in Ben's family, and evaluate the clinical and ethical options available to Ben and his wife regarding genetic testing for their children, prenatal diagnosis, and future reproductive technologies. [8 marks]
guidance: Molecular & Cellular Pathophysiology: Unstable CAG repeat expansion (>=40 repeats) in exon 1 of HTT (chr 4p16.3) causes polyglutamine expansion; mutant huntingtin misfolds (toxic gain-of-function), forming inclusion bodies, disrupting axonal transport and BDNF expression, triggering selective apoptosis of GABAergic medium spiny neurons (MSNs) in the striatum (caudate and putamen), leading to motor chorea [3 marks].

Genetic Anticipation Mechanism: DNA polymerase replication slippage during meiosis expands the CAG tract; paternal transmission bias during spermatogenesis causes substantial repeat expansion, conferring risk of earlier age of onset and greater severity in his offspring [2 marks].

Inheritance & Testing Evaluation: Autosomal dominant cross (Ben Hh x Wife hh) confers a 50% independent risk per pregnancy. Presymptomatic testing of minor children (aged 6 and 3) is ethically deferred until adulthood (age 18) to preserve autonomy and right not to know. For the unborn fetus, prenatal diagnosis (CVS/amniocentesis) carries miscarriage risk and raises abortion dilemmas. Pre-implantation Genetic Diagnosis (PGD/PGT-M) with IVF offers an embryo-screening alternative for future pregnancies [3 marks].

plenary: Huntington's disease exemplifies an autosomal dominant trinucleotide repeat disorder characterized by toxic gain-of-function and selective striatal MSN apoptosis.
Each child of an affected heterozygous parent faces an independent 50% transmission risk, with paternal transmission posing heightened risk of genetic anticipation.
Ethical clinical management balances predictive testing autonomy in minors against prenatal diagnosis (CVS/amniocentesis) and PGD-IVF options.
Mastery of Boolean database searching, CRAAP source evaluation, and Harvard referencing provides the foundational toolkit for high-scoring NEA coursework.

starterQuestions.q: What is the genotype of an individual affected by a heterozygous autosomal dominant disorder such as Huntington's disease?
starterQuestions.a: Hh (heterozygous, carrying one mutant expanded HTT allele and one normal allele).

starterQuestions.q: What is the mathematical probability that an affected heterozygous parent (Hh) transmits Huntington's disease to each biological child when mated with an unaffected partner (hh)?
starterQuestions.a: 50% (1 in 2, or a probability of 0.5) for each pregnancy, independent of the sex or health of previous children.

starterQuestions.q: Which specific trinucleotide triplet sequence undergoes pathological expansion in exon 1 of the HTT gene on chromosome 4p16.3?
starterQuestions.a: Cytosine-Adenine-Guanine (CAG), encoding an elongated polyglutamine (polyQ) tract.

starterQuestions.q: What is the diagnostic full-penetrance CAG repeat threshold for Huntington's disease?
starterQuestions.a: 40 or more CAG repeats (>=40 CAG repeats confers 100% lifetime penetrance of Huntington's disease).

starterQuestions.q: Which specific population of neurons within the basal ganglia undergoes selective degeneration in early-stage Huntington's disease?
starterQuestions.a: GABAergic Medium Spiny Neurons (MSNs) within the striatum (caudate nucleus and putamen).

starterQuestions.q: Why is genetic anticipation in Huntington's disease significantly more pronounced when the mutant allele is transmitted paternally rather than maternally?
starterQuestions.a: Continuous, lifelong meiotic cell divisions in spermatogenesis generate high rates of DNA replication slippage compared to oogenesis.
